Let me answer both questions.

1. Exporting individual clips from Adobe (Premiere Pro) for video reference

Quickest workflow for getting clean reference clips out of Premiere to feed into Seedance/Kling/Runway:

Method A — In/Out points + Export (cleanest, one clip at a time)

Set In point (I) at clip start, Out point (O) at clip end on the timeline

File → Export → Media (or Cmd+M / Ctrl+M)

Format: H.264, Preset: Match Source – High Bitrate (or YouTube 1080p Full HD)

Source Range: Sequence In/Out

Uncheck "Use Maximum Render Quality" only if you need speed

Export

Method B — Multiple clips at once via markers + Scene Edit Detection

If you have a long edit and need to chop it into shot-by-shot clips: select the clip, right-click → Scene Edit Detection → it cuts at every edit point automatically

Then select each segment, right-click → Export Frame for stills, or use the Out/In + Export Media for each

Faster route: install Multi-Camera Exporter or use Adobe Media Encoder's batch queue — drag each in/out range to the queue, hit Start Queue, walk away

Method C — Fastest for AI tool reference (what I'd actually do)

Just throw in/out points around the shot, hit Cmd+M, export as H.264 1080p

For Seedance/Kling references, you don't need ProRes — H.264 is fine and uploads faster

Keep them under ~10 seconds where possible since most AI video tools cap at 5–10s reference video

If you're working in After Effects instead of Premiere: Composition → Add to Render Queue → output module set to H.264 → render. Or use Adobe Media Encoder via Composition → Add to Adobe Media Encoder Queue.

2. Seedance vs Kling for Shot 1 — and the actual prompt

Quick answer: Use Kling 3.0 Motion Control for this shot, not Seedance.

Here's why, based on what you're trying to do:

Your shot has a specific human performance you've already filmed — the hand closing the iPad, the camera tilt-up reveal, the character standing and grabbing the bag. You don't want to regenerate that performance from scratch. You want to preserve the choreography and camera move and apply the 2.5D stylized look on top.

That's exactly what Kling 3.0 Motion Control was built for — it takes your reference performance video and a stylized character/environment design image, and regenerates the scene with your exact motion + camera path applied to the styled version.

Seedance is better when you have no live-action plate and need the AI to invent the motion (previz, pure AI inserts, transformation sequences). For your hybrid workflow where the live plate is the foundation, Kling is the right tool here.

That said — Seedance's First/Last Frame mode can do this too, and it's worth testing as a backup or for the parts where you want more AI freedom. So I'll give you both.

Option A — Kling 3.0 Motion Control (recommended for Shot 1)

Inputs:

Reference video: Your live-action plate of Shot 1 (top-down iPad close → tilt-up reveal → character grabs bag)

Reference image: Your stylized hero keyframe — the 2.5D illustrated version of the character in the classroom (the second image you uploaded works as this anchor)

Prompt:

Apply the visual style of the reference image to the motion in the reference video. 
Maintain the exact camera movement, timing, and character choreography from the video.

A young man in an orange Nike sweatshirt, black Nike cap, glasses, and beard sits at a 
classroom desk. The shot opens top-down on his iPad in a black folio case, an Apple Pencil 
beside it — the screen shows handwritten notes on a grid background. His hand enters frame 
and closes the iPad cover. The camera tilts up smoothly from the desk to reveal the 
character at eye level. He stands, slings his black backpack over one shoulder, and turns 
toward the classroom door. Behind him, a green chalkboard covered in equations and the 
words "chaos outside / peace inside" written in chalk. Empty desks and chairs in soft warm 
classroom light, late afternoon mood.

2.5D stylized illustration, hand-drawn line work, painterly cel-shading, muted warm 
palette, soft rim light from the windows.

Why this works: Kling will lock onto your camera move and the character's exact motion, and only restyle the rendering. Your continuity (the same actor, same performance, same iPad-to-bag beat) is preserved.

Option B — Seedance 2.0 First/Last Frame (backup / test)

If you want to try Seedance as well — especially because you already have both reference frames as stills — use First/Last Frame pinning. This is closer to forcing the AI to invent the motion between two frames you control.

Inputs:

<<<image_1>>> — top-down iPad shot (your start frame)

<<<image_2>>> — character standing with backpack (your end frame, the second upload)

Prompt:

Use <<<image_1>>> as the exact starting frame. Use <<<image_2>>> as the exact final frame.
Do not change either image. The video must start matching Image 1 and end matching Image 2 perfectly.

Continuous handheld shot, 2.5D stylized illustration, hand-drawn line work, painterly 
cel-shading. Open top-down on the iPad — a young man's hand enters frame from the right 
and closes the black folio cover over the screen. As the cover snaps shut, the camera 
tilts up smoothly along the desk, rising past the chalkboard with equations and the 
words "chaos outside / peace inside," and settles at eye level on the character — orange 
Nike sweatshirt, black cap, glasses, beard, black backpack already over one shoulder, 
turning toward the classroom door.

Soft warm classroom light, late afternoon mood, gentle camera shake. 
Sound: paper rustle, the soft click of the iPad cover, chair scraping back, fabric 
shuffle of the backpack strap, footsteps starting on tile.

Ratio: 16:9 | Duration: 8s | Resolution: 1080p | Audio: on

Heads up on Seedance for this shot: the camera move (top-down → tilt-up to eye-level reveal) is aggressive — the AI has to invent ~180° of vertical reframing between two very different compositions. First/Last Frame can do it, but you'll likely need 2–4 generations to get a clean one. The bag-grab and turn might also get lost or smoothed over since it's a lot of action for an 8s pin.

My recommendation for you

For Shot 1 specifically:

Primary: Run it through Kling 3.0 Motion Control with your live-action plate + a stylized character keyframe. Cleanest path because your performance is preserved.

Backup test: Burn 1–2 Seedance First/Last Frame generations as comparison. If Kling gives you the motion fidelity but Seedance gives you a more striking stylization on a specific frame, you can mix.

Don't try to regenerate this shot from text alone — you've already got the performance on camera, lean on it.

Got it — the failure mode you're describing is classic: the model holds the start frame's style, drifts into the live-plate's photographic look in the middle, then snaps to the end frame's style at the last moment. The middle isn't getting styled.

Two things fix this. Stronger style anchoring in the prompt (explicit "all frames" lock language) and more style reference images so the model has multiple anchors instead of just two endpoints.

What to do

For Kling 2.5 Turbo Pro — Start/End Frame mode:

Kling's start/end mode only takes 2 images (the two endpoints). You can't add extra style refs in this mode. So the only lever is the prompt itself — make the style lock explicit and aggressive.

Top-down on the iPad. A hand enters from below and closes the folio cover, then lifts 
the tablet up and out of frame. Camera pulls back and tilts up as the character stands 
from the chair, slings his backpack over his shoulder, and turns left toward the door.

Maintain the exact 2.5D hand-drawn illustrated style of both reference frames across 
every single frame of the video — painterly cel-shading, ink line work, muted warm 
palette. No photographic frames. No live-action look. The entire shot must look like 
an animated illustration from start to finish.

The "no photographic frames / no live-action look" line is the critical addition — it tells the model what not to drift toward.

For Seedance — where you can actually add style reference images:

This is where Seedance has an advantage over Kling for your problem. Seedance accepts up to 9 reference images, and the tutorial in your project specifically showed that adding more style anchors fixes mid-clip drift.

Setup:

<<<image_1>>> — first frame (top-down iPad, stylized)

<<<image_2>>> — last frame (character with backpack, stylized)

<<<image_3>>> — extra style anchor (a clean stylized still — your shot1.png master keyframe, or any of the strongest stylized character frames you have)

<<<image_4>>> — another stylized environment frame (classroom interior in the same style)

<<<video_1>>> — your live plate for motion reference

Prompt:

<<<video_1>>> is the motion and camera reference — match its exact camera move and 
character choreography. <<<image_1>>> is the exact starting frame. <<<image_2>>> is 
the exact final frame. Do not change either image. <<<image_3>>> and <<<image_4>>> 
define the visual style — apply this style to every frame of the video.

Top-down on the iPad. A hand enters from below, closes the folio cover, then lifts 
the tablet up and out of frame. The camera pulls back and tilts up as the character 
stands from the chair, slings his black backpack over his shoulder, and turns left 
toward the door.

Sound: paper rustle, the soft click of the iPad folio closing, chair leg scraping on 
tile, fabric shuffle of the backpack strap, the first footstep.

Lock the 2.5D hand-drawn illustrated style of <<<image_3>>> across every frame — 
painterly cel-shading, ink line work, muted warm palette. No photographic or 
live-action frames anywhere in the video.

Ratio: 16:9 | Resolution: 1080p | Audio: on

Why this works for the drift problem

The issue you hit before is that with only <<<video_1>>> + 2 endpoint frames, Seedance had 3 inputs telling it the photographic look (the entire video) and 2 inputs telling it the illustrated look (the endpoint stills). The math was against you. The model averaged toward the video's look in the middle.

By adding 2–4 extra stylized stills as pure style references (reference_image role, not first_frame/last_frame), you flip that ratio. Now the model sees more illustrated anchors than photographic ones, and the explicit "no photographic frames" line in the prompt blocks the drift path.

My recommendation for which tool to use

For this specific shot, with the drift problem you're describing:

Kling 2.5 Turbo Pro start/end frame if you trust the prompt-only style lock and want simplicity. Faster iteration, cleaner motion, but less control over middle-frame style.

Seedance 2.0 with video + 4 image refs if you want to actually solve the drift. More setup, but the multi-image anchor approach directly attacks the failure mode you described.

Given you've already hit the drift problem once, I'd go Seedance with 4 style refs for this shot. Run 2–3 generations and pick the best.
